quiz.title: Module 1 — Editing with Rhythm
quiz.description: Monday's quiz covers pacing, timing and visual rhythm, shot selection and continuity, camera angles, and cutting on movement and action.

questions.prompt: What is the potential problem with cutting scenes too quickly?
options: It automatically lowers the video's resolution.
It makes every scene feel emotional.
It can confuse viewers and make it difficult for them to follow what is happening.
It prevents the editor from adding music.
questions.explanation: Pace has to serve understanding. Cut too quickly and the viewer loses the thread of what is happening, however energetic the edit feels.

questions.prompt: According to the first transcript, what is an important consideration when deciding how long a shot should remain on screen?
options: Whether the shot contributes to the story, emotion, or understanding of the scene.
Whether every shot lasts exactly 2.5 seconds.
Whether the video contains at least five transitions.
Whether the editor can avoid using close-up shots.
questions.explanation: Shot duration is a judgement about purpose, not a fixed number. A shot earns its time on screen by contributing to the story, the emotion, or the viewer's understanding.

questions.prompt: Which type of shot is primarily used to establish where a scene takes place?
options: Extreme close-up
Cowboy shot
Medium close-up
Establishing shot
questions.explanation: An establishing shot sets the scene — it shows the audience where they are before narrowing in on the action.

questions.prompt: A filmmaker wants to make a character appear powerful and dominant in a scene. Which camera angle would best support this intention?
options: High-angle shot
Low-angle shot
Extreme close-up
Over-the-shoulder shot
questions.explanation: A low-angle shot looks up at the subject, which makes them appear larger and more dominant. A high angle does the opposite.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a close-up and an extreme close-up?
options: A close-up shows multiple people, while an extreme close-up shows only one person.
A close-up establishes a location, while an extreme close-up shows the full body.
A close-up can show a character's face from the chin upward, while an extreme close-up focuses on a much smaller detail, such as the eyes.
A close-up is always filmed from above, while an extreme close-up is filmed from below.
questions.explanation: Both are tight, but the extreme close-up goes closer still — from the face to a single detail such as the eyes.

questions.prompt: An editor is creating a 30-second promotional video and needs to communicate information quickly. Which approach would be most appropriate?
options: Leave long periods of dead space between clips.
Avoid cutting footage until the video reaches its final seconds.
Use the same shot duration throughout the entire video, regardless of the content.
Remove unnecessary dead space and use concise cuts while keeping the information clear.
questions.explanation: In a short piece, every second has to work. Trim the dead space and cut concisely — but keep the information clear, because speed that loses the message is not useful.

questions.prompt: What does OTS mean in filmmaking, and why is this shot commonly used?
options: Over the shoulder; it helps present conversations with added depth and visual interest.
On the screen; it helps increase the video's resolution.
Outside the scene; it establishes the location of a film.
Object tracking shot; it automatically follows moving objects during editing.
questions.explanation: OTS stands for over the shoulder. Framing past one person's shoulder towards another gives a conversation depth and puts the viewer in the space.

questions.prompt: A director wants the audience to feel that a character is disoriented and that something is wrong in the scene. Which shot could help create this feeling?
options: Full shot
Dutch angle
Establishing shot
Group shot
questions.explanation: A Dutch angle tilts the horizon, and that imbalance unsettles the viewer — a natural choice when something is meant to feel wrong.
